S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral disturbances within three months of an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with distress out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor and/or significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The presentation is heterogeneous and can include anxious, depressed, or mixed emotional features, as well as maladaptive behavioral responses such as withdrawal, conflict, or decline in role performance. By definition, the disturbance does not represent normal bereavement, does not meet criteria for another mental disorder, and symptoms do not persist for more than six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended. It is often seen in the context of life transitions, interpersonal conflicts, health problems, or occupational stress, and is distinguished from more severe mood or anxiety disorders by its time-limited, stressor-linked course and relatively circumscribed impairment.

patient.personality: Amy is a highly organized, routine‑oriented woman who takes pride in precision, reliability, and keeping her environment and responsibilities meticulously ordered.
patient.stressor: Amy had managed her health fairly well into her mid‑80s, structuring her days around work at the senior center, church, and familiar home routines, when she experienced a sudden fall on her front steps that resulted in a hip fracture and brief hospitalization. Although the surgery went well, she was told she would need to use a walker for several months and cut back significantly on her front‑desk duties, and her husband and adult children began gently insisting she not live alone at home during her recovery. For someone who has built her identity around independence, punctuality, and being the dependable point‑person at the senior center, the abrupt loss of mobility and control over her schedule—with others now rearranging her medications, appointments, and even her kitchen—felt deeply unsettling, and over the next month she struggled to reconcile the imposed changes with her need for order and self‑reliance, leading her to increasingly rigid and strained attempts to maintain her old routines. When staff at the senior center noticed that her distress about minor scheduling changes and perceived mistakes was escalating and beginning to interfere with her ability to enjoy her hobbies and interact calmly with others, her primary care physician recommended a psychiatric evaluation to help her adjust to the health-related changes.
patient.chief_complaint: “Since I broke my hip and everyone started changing my routines, I just haven’t been coping with all the stress the way I usually can.”

S081.manifestation: Ever since the fall, I find myself snapping at my family for moving things or changing my appointment times, then crying about it later, and I keep pushing myself to stick to my old work and house routines even though my hip and this walker make it impossible, which just leaves me exhausted and upset with everyone, including myself.
